awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a New Manufacturing Method for Petroleum-based Polyacrylonitrile Specialty Acrylic Fibers
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the translation from lab to market of a manufacturing solution to affordably produce acrylic fibers in the U.S. This solution addresses the current reliance on imported acrylic fibers, especially given their importance in manufacturing military, outdoor, and apparel applications. The commercialization of this solution has the potential to benefit the U.S. economy and society by introducing competitively priced acrylic fibers that are domestically made. The acrylic fiber market is worth $1 billion annually. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a more affordable method of manufacturing petroleum-based polyacrylonitrile (PAN) into specialty acrylic fibers and precursors to carbon fiber. The current process of spinning PAN-based fibers relies on volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are flammable and toxic. This new solution consists of manufacturing PAN-based fibers by the process of melt spinning at high speed, offering a low energy approach to fiber manufacturing. The benefits of this approach include a reliable, domestic supply of acrylic fibers for U.S. textile fiber mills at a potentially lower cost.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Participation in the NSF I-CORPS program enabled our team to explore the commercial viability of our innovation for spinning fibers from the plastic called poly(acrylonitrile) or PAN. This plastic is used to make fibers known for their wool-like behavior. Further, these PAN fibers can be turned into carbon fiber through high temperature processing. Carbon fibers are useful due to their high strength, high modulus, temperature resistance and density less than steel and aluminum metals. Our team addressed the intellectual merits of this project by conducting over 100 interviews, attending conferences, and major industry gatherings across the material supply chain (from vendor to potential customer). People were interviewed to understand

  • How potential partners/customers perceive the cost-benefit of sustainable manufacturing
  • Whether sectors of the textile industry prioritize the purchase of ‘Made in the US’ products
  • Whether the textile industry anticipates legislation that will limit or penalize the use of chemicals that may have some levels of toxicity

By touring manufacturing and testing facilities, our team was also able to make more informed decisions about our business and pricing models. By engaging in NSF I-CORPS programming, our team was able to target customers for early adoption and high-volume markets.

The broader impacts of the proposed innovation include:

  • Reducing the hazards associated with PAN fibers
  • Enabling the onshoring of PAN fiber spinning in the US

Several interviewees showed excitement over the potential to show impact in these areas. On-shoring may also result in shorter lead times and lower minimum quantities per order for customers.
